title: Is reciting the Quran in Arabic without understanding rewarding?
headline: Reciting the Quran in Arabic without understanding earns reward, while reflection adds a further rank

summary.text: The four schools agree that reciting the Quran in Arabic is rewarded even without understanding the meaning, while reflection adds a separate and higher reward. The fatwas cited treat the reward of recitation and the reward of understanding as distinct, not rivals. The Prophet ﷺ modelled a reading that stopped at meaning, pausing at verses of mercy and punishment.

paragraphs.text: The Quran asks for reflection on its verses, as in the command "Then do they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?" (47:24) and "a blessed Book which We have revealed to you, that they might reflect upon its verses" (38:29). Al-Qurtubi took 47:24 as proof that reflection is required in order to know its meaning. The command to "recite it with its true recital" (2:121) is glossed in the verse's own footnote as applying its teachings, and 73:4 orders measured recitation, while 7:204 orders attentive listening.

In the two-rewards hadith of Aisha, the skilled reciter is with the noble scribes, and the one who stumbles and finds it hard has two rewards. It is in Sahih al-Bukhari 4937, Sahih Muslim 798a as quoted by al-Uthaymeen, Sunan Abi Dawud 1454, Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2904, Sunan Ibn Majah 3779 and Sunan ad-Darimi 3234; al-Albani and Shu'ayb al-Arnaut's colleagues graded the Abu Dawud route sahih, and the Tirmidhi route is graded sahih or hasan sahih by its editors. The letter hadith of Ibn Mas'ud promises ten good deeds per letter, with "Alif-Lam-Mim" counted as three letters; at-Tirmidhi graded it hasan sahih and its editors graded it sahih.

"He who recites the Qur'an in less than three days has not understood it" was graded hasan sahih by at-Tirmidhi and sahih by the collection's editors, linking pace to comprehension. The Khawarij warning describes a people who "recite the Qur'an with their tongues, but it does not go beyond their collarbones" (Sahih Muslim 1068a), censuring recitation that stops at the throat. "Recite the Qur'an, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions" (Sahih Muslim, in Riyad as-Salihin 991) and "The best among you are those who learn the Qur'an and teach it" (Sahih al-Bukhari 5028) commend recitation and teaching.

The Prophet ﷺ recited slowly and deliberately, glorifying at verses of glorification and asking at verses of request, as Hudhayfah described praying behind him one night; Abu Dawud's report adds that his bowing matched his standing in length. Umm Salamah described him pausing verse by verse, a report al-Albani and Muhammad Muhyi al-Din Abdul Hamid graded sahih, while Zubair Ali Zai graded it da'if.

The Hanafi Ibn Abidin states in Radd al-Muhtar that "the aim in reciting the Quran is the Quran itself" (المقصود من قراءة القرآن عين القرآن), unlike a book whose aim is grasping its content, in the chapter on oaths. The same work repeatedly rules that recitation done for payment carries no reward for reciter or deceased, that hiring for mere tilawah was not held by any imam, and that the later jurists allowed payment for teaching, not reciting.

The Shafi'i Mughni al-Muhtaj cites 47:24 for tartil and answering verses of mercy and punishment, recommends reciting "with reflection and humility," and holds reading from the mushaf better than reciting from memory. It records Ibn Mas'ud's ten-verse method and explains that "the most reciting" (al-aqra') in the hadith means the most understanding of the Quran. The Shafi'i manual also reports al-Qadi Husayn's dislike of speed in recitation.

The Maliki al-Dasuqi's hashiyah records the madhhab's position that recitation's reward does not reach the dead, with three views reported. Mukhtasar Khalil lists as disliked in prayer a specific supplication or one in non-Arabic for a person able to do otherwise, and al-Madunah reports Malik's dislike of a man sitting so people gather for him to recite.

The Hanbali Kashshaf al-Qina' states plainly that "understanding the Quran and reflecting on it with the heart is better than reciting it much without understanding" (والتفهم في القرآن والتدبر بالقلب منه أفضل من إدراجه كثيرًا بغير تفهم), citing 38:29. Ibn Qudama's al-Mughni rules that one who cannot recite in Arabic must learn, and otherwise his prayer is invalid.

The tension is between verses blaming those who do not reflect and hadiths promising ten rewards per letter regardless. The scholars cited resolve it by distinguishing two things that can both be present: the reward of tilawah, which is not conditional on comprehension, and the reward of tadabbur and action, which comprehension adds.

Ibn al-Qayyim, quoted by IslamQA, reports the disagreement over whether slow recitation with reflection and little quantity is better than fast recitation with much, noting that Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas held the former better. He resolves it by saying the reward of tartil and tadabbur is greater in rank while the reward of quantity is greater in number, the first like giving a precious jewel, the second like giving many dirhams. The Hanbali and Shafi'i manuals make the same ranking without denying the lesser reward.

The Khawarij hadith and Ibn al-Qayyim's comparison of the hypocrite who recites to a sweet-smelling herb with a bitter taste function as a warning about stopping at the tongue, not as a denial that recitation is rewarded. Al-Uthaymeen put it that the reciter "is not a loser no matter what; he is a winner in all cases."

The Permanent Committee (Fatwa 15856) answered that reciting with contemplation yields a greater reward, since one obtains the reward of recitation and of contemplation, "and if one recites it without understanding its meaning and without contemplating it, he has the reward for recitation," citing the letter hadith. In Fatwa 19596 it called the claim that a reciter who does not know the interpretation is sinful "a clear error" requiring repentance, and affirmed that such recitation is "among the righteous deeds for which one is rewarded." Fatwa 17775 added that recitation is better than listening, and recitation with reflection better than without.

Al-Uthaymeen said a person is rewarded whether he understands the meaning or not, but "it is not befitting for a believer to read the Qur'an... without understanding its meaning," and directed him to trustworthy tafsir. He explained the two rewards as the reward of recitation plus the reward of effort, quoting the Prophet's words to Aisha, "Your reward is according to your effort" (أجرك على قدر نصبك), and noted that hardship in worship brings greater reward than ease. He also held there is no recitation-reward for merely following the page with the eyes, since recitation requires moving the lips and tongue.

Egypt's Dar al-Ifta, in Fatwa 7046 dated 27 June 1991 from Dr Muhammad Sayyid Tantawi, concluded from the two-rewards hadith and the general texts that the virtue and reward of reciting are established "whether he is skilled in reciting it and knowledgeable of its meanings or not," quoting al-Nawawi's explanation that the faltering reciter has a reward for recitation and a reward for his stumbling and hardship. Darul Uloom Deoband (Fatwa 1499/1064, 2012) answered that the hadith establishes reward for reciting "whether one understands or not"; ShariahBoard's mufti said there is "no condition and restriction of reciting with the understanding," calling this the position of the reliable scholars; Askimam stated the reciter is rewarded tenfold per letter "regardless if it is recited with understanding or without understanding"; and Fatwa.ca framed recitation as an independent act of worship, distinct from understanding and from acting. Ibn Baz, in the answer carried by IslamQA, said it is permissible to recite without understanding while reflection remains the goal.

On translations, the answer is narrower: the letter-reward is tied to the Arabic text, and there is no textual proof that reading a translation earns the same reward, though reading it to understand and benefit is praiseworthy and rewarded. The practical upshot in the fatwas is consistent: recite in Arabic, expect the reward, and treat understanding as the goal you grow toward, through tafsir and trustworthy scholars.
